title: Delegation and Interface Reuse
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of delegation and interface reuse in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply delegation and interface reuse in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to keeping mixins small and predictable and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Delegation and Interface Reuse through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding delegation and interface reuse helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Delegation and Interface Reuse helps you reason about delegating to collaborator objects. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Delegating to collaborator objects. Then connect it to Explicit public interfaces. The remaining syllabus points—Keeping mixins small and predictable—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Delegation and Interface Reuse
content_blocks.code:
module Timestamped
  def timestamp_label
    "created at: #{Time.now.year}"
  end
end
class Report
  include Timestamped
end
puts Report.new.timestamp_label

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports delegation and interface reuse. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for delegation and interface reuse using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Keeping mixins small and predictable), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain delegation and interface reuse, identify its place in modules, mixins, and code organization, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
